doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Murray the teacher and his books
summary: Thomas visits Murray in Harlem and describes his books, including The Omni-Americans and Stomping the Blues, and Murray's view of the blues.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: He said that to me, yeah. But see Murray was, to some he was very cantankerous, argumentative you know. But he was at heart a teacher. I mean he taught at a number of schools but there were just people who he took under his wing and he was patient in his professorial and teacherly capacity. So I would go over to his place on 132nd off Lenox Avenue, which those of us who are Murrayites call the spyglass tree. That’s one of his phrases. You know you have the little spyglass, you go into a tree and you have a spyglass that gave you a view of whatever you’re looking at in a closer view. And The Spyglass Tree is the name of one of his novels. His second novel. I would talk to him, I would interview him, I read his work. He put me on to Michael James, who I mentioned earlier, and Michael and I became very close. So I consider myself a Murrayite in that sense. So his work is fundamental. In fact I’m about to do some work, some books dealing with his thought in more detail. So he wrote books like The Omni-Americans which I think if people would take a look at that book called The Omni-Americans more seriously they would have a richer conception of what being an Americans means and they would look much less at race and more towards culture. Okay. The Omni-American means all-American, but his point was that being an American means that you’re going to have some kind of mixed mulatto something most of the time. And that’s okay. Because most of us are mixed in some kind of way or another, you know, the genetic works that Henry Louis Gates is doing through some companies, and these shows that he has on PBS where he looks at the genetic history of usually famous people shows that these mixtures are just reality. Murray also wrote The Hero and the Blues, which takes a look at the blues and heroism from a literary context. He has Stomping the Blues, which is like a poetic of the blues which talks about the blues kind of every which way, looking at it © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

from the sacred and secular perspective, looking at it from a historical territory bands to the icons and heroes of the cannon. He also wrote, and this is non-fiction I’m talking about, the autobiography of Count Basie you know, Good Morning Blues, as told to Albert Murray. The Blue Devils of Nada, a contemporary approach to the American Aesthetic Statement I think it’s called, and a book of poetry, four novels from Train Whistle Guitar, which he worked on for a long time, which I think may be his classic of fictional work, to The Spyglass Tree, which takes the main character, Scooter, who we are introduced to through Train Whistle Guitar and he’s in college in [The] Spyglass Tree. Then you have The Seven League Boots where the main character is now an adult, a young adult, and he ends up going on the road with a character named the Bossman. And the Bossman is kind of a combination of Basie and Ellington and he’s playing bass. And his last novel, The Magic Keys. So he was a great writer, an original thinker who, if more — if he were better known and his work were better known I think he would not only change the discourse and the conversation regarding race and taking it more in the direction of culture but it would also clarify things regarding the meaning and significance of blues in jazz, not only in American history but as a dynamic that really has been a powerful, has had such a powerful impact around the world. I mean just to give you one example, it was Murray who clarified that the blues as such as he calls it, is about you know, a sorrowful situation of being downtrodden and that kind of thing. But blues music is not about that. Blues music is part of a communal and ritual practice that allow people to actually counter, “stomp the blues.” And he puts it in the context of when you have blues music and you’re feeling good and you’re dancing and stuff, that’s part of like courtship rituals and leads to a fertility ritual, so we can perpetuate the species. So that’s taking it out to like a very fundamental anthropological level. But a lot of people don’t understand that. I mean I didn’t understand that in high school. I was like the blues, all right. You know, talking about the blues and slavery, I don’t want to deal with that.
